sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go's net/http package is powerful enough to serve production traffic at scale without any framework — the Go team's own services, Docker, and many cloud-native tools are built on it directly. Understanding stdlib HTTP is a prerequisite for understanding any framework built on top of it, and interviewers use this topic to test whether a candidate actually understands the abstractions versus just knowing a framework's API. Misconfigured http.Server timeouts and http.Client misuse are two of the most common production incidents in Go services.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: `http.Handler` is a single-method interface — `ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request)` — and is the fundamental composition unit for the entire HTTP ecosystem. `http.HandlerFunc` is a function type that implements Handler, letting you use any `func(w, r)` directly as a handler. `http.ServeMux` is the standard router — it matches URL patterns and dispatches to registered handlers; Go 1.22 added method routing (`GET /foo`) and wildcard segments (`/users/{id}`). Middleware is just a function that takes a Handler and returns a Handler, forming a chain.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **http.Handler and http.HandlerFunc**: the core interface and its function adapter — every framework implements Handler under the hood.
- **ServeMux routing**: `mux.Handle` and `mux.HandleFunc`; Go 1.22+ patterns like `GET /users/{id}`; more specific patterns win over less specific.
- **Middleware pattern**: `func Logging(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return http.HandlerFunc(func(w, r) { log...; next.ServeHTTP(w, r) }) }` — compose by wrapping.
- **http.Client with Transport**: `http.Client` is goroutine-safe and should be shared (not created per request); Transport manages the connection pool.
- **Server timeouts**: `ReadTimeout`, `WriteTimeout`, `IdleTimeout`, `ReadHeaderTimeout` — all must be set on `http.Server` in production to prevent goroutine leaks from slow/malicious clients.
- **http.DefaultServeMux**: global mutable state — any imported package can register routes on it; use `http.NewServeMux()` for applications.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Creating new http.Client per request**: allocates a new Transport per call, bypassing connection pooling, rapidly exhausting file descriptors under load — always share a single client.
- **Missing server timeouts**: a client that connects but sends the request infinitely slowly holds a goroutine for as long as the connection lives; `ReadHeaderTimeout` is the most important mitigation.
- **http.DefaultServeMux in production**: third-party packages (including Go's own net/http/pprof) register handlers on DefaultServeMux at import time, accidentally exposing debug endpoints if you use it.
- **ResponseWriter must be written in order**: write headers before calling Write; once Write is called, headers are flushed and WriteHeader is a no-op.
- **Request body must be read and closed**: failing to read (or drain) and close the Body leaks the TCP connection back to the pool.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "In Go I implement middleware by wrapping http.Handler — a middleware function takes a handler and returns a new handler that does some work before or after calling the inner handler's ServeHTTP. I always create a custom ServeMux with http.NewServeMux rather than using the default global mux, to avoid accidentally sharing routes with imported packages. For the http.Server I always set ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, and IdleTimeout — without them a slow client can hold open a goroutine indefinitely and exhaust server resources. On the client side I create one shared http.Client at startup and reuse it everywhere, because each Client owns a Transport that manages connection pooling, and creating one per request bypasses that entirely."
